extraction.research_question: How to reach a consensus in large-scale group decision-making (LSGDM) with social networks (SN-LSGDM) when decision-makers (DMs) submit incomplete fuzzy preference relations (IFPRs), while minimizing unit adjustment cost (UAC) and keeping trust relations dynamic. Sub-questions: (a) estimate missing preference entries using K-nearest neighbours in the trust network; (b) cluster DMs into subgroups using trust, preference similarity and UAC; (c) run a two-stage (individual and subgroup) feedback consensus process based on three-way decision (TWD) with a cost-minimizing optimization step.
extraction.theory: Consensus reaching process (CRP) with soft consensus; minimum-adjustment-cost feedback (Ben-Arieh and Easton 2007; unit adjustment cost); social trust networks and fuzzy sociometry (Wasserman and Faust 1994; Dong et al. 2018); additive consistency of fuzzy preference relations (Tanino 1984; Xu et al. 2017); K-nearest neighbour estimation (Cover and Hart 1967); three-way decision (Yao 2010) mapping DMs into Pos, Bnd and Neg regions via a comprehensive adjustment priority (CAP) threshold. The paper argues trust should drive both imputation and adjustment; no formal theorem or convergence proof is given.
extraction.data: Illustrative case (Sec. 5.1, p.11): venture-capital diversified investment, 20 DMs (e1-e20), 5 alternatives (x1-x5: green logistics, ecological materials, digital economy, sustainable energy, machine learning). 20 incomplete 5x5 fuzzy preference matrices with 39 missing entries. Standardized evaluation matrices and trust network are taken from Gong et al. (2024) and are not reproduced; the paper points to a GitHub repository and says "Data will be made available on request" (p.19). UAC values for the 20 DMs were generated randomly by a program and are listed in Sec. 6.1.2 (p.14). No calendar period is stated. Simulation (Sec. 6.2, p.15-16): DM count 50 to 5000 in steps of 50, 5 alternatives, randomly generated data. Robustness test (Sec. 6.3, p.16): p in {20,40,60,80,100}, n in {4,6,8,10,12}, missing probability 0.1/0.2/0.3, 10 repetitions per cell, synthetic data.
extraction.method:
Four-part model. (1) Missing-value estimation (Sec. 3.1, Defs 3.1-3.6, Eqs 11-19): find K trusted neighbours with known entry; similarity sim_K (Eqs 12-13) and membership mu (Eq 14, mu = (t + sim)/(1 + sim)); normalize to weights (Eq 15); reliability r (Eq 16); impute f = sum of weights times neighbour values (Eqs 17-18), filling highest-reliability entries first and iterating to convergence. Complexity O(K^2 n p) (Remark 3.2). (2) Improved k-means on the trust network (Sec. 3.2, Defs 3.7-3.8, Eqs 20-30): trust influence Int(e_u) (Eq 20); adaptive k and initial centroids via a trust-discrepancy threshold (Eqs 21-23, Algorithm 1); distance = comprehensive difference combining (1 - mutual influence) and |UAC_u - UAC_v| / 2 (Eqs 24-29); iterate to SSE convergence (Algorithm 2, Eq 30). Complexity O(k n p^2) (Remark 3.5). (3) TWD consensus (Sec. 4.1, Def 4.1, Eqs 31-33): Pos = DMs with CD >= theta_ideal; CAP_r = beta(1 - UAC_r) + ((1-beta)/2) t_r + ((1-beta)/2)(1 - CD_r) (Eq 32); threshold CAP_lambda = CAP_min + lambda(CAP_max - CAP_min) (Eq 33); Neg if CAP >= CAP_lambda else Bnd. (4) Two-stage optimization (Sec. 4.2, Eqs 34-40): stage 1 minimizes sum of UAC_u times sum |h_ij - f_ij| over Neg DMs subject to Pos-based trust-weighted adjustment constraints, solved as a linear program (Python linprog); trust update t* = t^(1 - t) (Eqs 35-36, 39-40); stage 2 repeats with subgroups as units (Eq 38). Stop when group consensus degree (GCD) >= theta_ideal. Overall complexity stated as O(k n p^2) (Remark 4.2). Parameters: beta = 0.4, lambda = 0.5, theta_ideal = 0.92, K = 4 (Sec. 5.1, p.11).</method>

limitations: Additive consistency of the input FPRs is assumed acceptable and not analysed (Sec. 2.1, p.5).
Non-cooperative behaviour is not modelled; the authors list it as future work (Sec. 7, p.18).
The authors state the optimization models cannot reach final consensus in a single iteration and plan to revise the objectives (Sec. 7, p.18).
Trust is the only factor used to pull dissenting DMs toward the group; other factors (expertise, track record, social influence) are deferred (Sec. 7, p.18-19).
The worked example uses one case with 20 DMs and 5 alternatives; larger groups are only simulated with random data (Sec. 5.1 p.11; Sec. 6.2 p.15).
UAC values are randomly generated by a program, not observed (Step 1, p.11; Sec. 6.1.2 p.14).
Parameters beta=0.4, lambda=0.5 and theta_ideal=0.92 are set by the authors' judgement; only K and beta are swept, and lambda and theta are not swept (Sec. 5.1, p.11; Sec. 6.1.2, p.15).
Quantitative comparison is against one method (M1) in one case with a figure only; the rest of the comparison is qualitative (Table 2, Sec. 6.4, p.16-18).

Cost-reduction claims versus the control group rely on figures (Fig 5, Fig 7) with no numeric totals in the text.
Real data are not included; the case relies on Gong et al. (2024) and a GitHub link; 'Data will be made available on request' (p.19).

summary_md:
Zhan and Cai (ESWA 2025) propose a consensus procedure for large groups whose members state incomplete fuzzy preference matrices and are linked by a trust network. It has four parts. (1) Missing preference entries are filled from the K most trusted neighbours who have that entry. Each neighbour is weighted by trust and preference similarity, the most reliable gaps are filled first, and filling repeats until stable. (2) Members are clustered with an adaptive k-means whose distance combines trust and unit adjustment cost (UAC). (3) A three-way decision rule sorts members into Pos, Bnd and Neg regions. (4) A two-stage linear program makes the cheapest preference adjustments, first per member and then per subgroup, until group consensus reaches 0.92.

All evidence is either one worked case or synthetic. The case has 20 decision-makers and 5 alternatives; its UAC values are random, and its trust network and preference data come from an earlier paper and are not reproduced. Group consensus rises from 0.9117 to 0.9368 over 11 rounds. The imputation MSE of 0.09 to 0.13 is measured only on randomly generated matrices. The paper compares numerically against one method, in a figure only. There is no causal identification, no holdout and no proof that the procedure converges.

The paper models committee-style preference aggregation. It does not model lobbying, legislators or influence, so most of Paul's systems are unaffected. Its one useful contact is network-neighbour imputation. The paper's estimator weights neighbours by tie strength and similarity and orders fills by reliability. The system's stance-dynamics proposer takes a plain mean over binary cosponsor neighbours. The extension is only worth testing because that same component found co-movement null on cosponsor ties. That null undercuts the homophily premise this whole imputation family relies on, and the paper never tests the premise on real data. Its "trust" is an elicited trust score, not cosponsorship. Reading cosponsor weights as trust would break D-025.

bearings.paper_claim: Missing preference entries are imputed from the K=4 most trusted neighbours with a known value. Each weight blends trust and preference similarity (mu = (t + sim)/(1 + sim), then normalized), and entries are filled in order of reliability r and iterated to convergence. In the worked case f10_45 = 0.4033 comes from 4 neighbours weighted 0.2549/0.2507/0.2503/0.2440, the highest-reliability gap (r = 3.8683) of 39 missing entries. Imputation MSE stays at 0.09-0.13 across p in {20..100}, n in {4..12} and missing rates 0.1/0.2/0.3, on synthetic data only.
bearings.system_side: The silent-member proposer takes each member's cosponsor neighbours as an UNWEIGHTED binary adjacency set (edge weights are dropped when the Edges sheet is read). It averages the neighbours' tier scores per category, with no similarity weighting, no reliability ordering and no iteration. It proposes a cell only when there are at least 5 neighbours (SD_MINNB) and |est| >= 0.75 (SD_CONF). It checks sign agreement on cells whose stance is already known, with no party-only baseline, and outputs proposals only. The same script reports co-movement as null on cosponsor ties.
bearings.code_ref: fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:89-93 (binary adj from cosponsor Edges); fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:132-147 (MINNB 5, CONF 0.75, unweighted mean, proposal-only); fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:94-110 (co-movement test)
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the mechanics carry over: neighbour weights from tie strength plus profile similarity, and filling the best-supported gaps first. The paper's evidence does not transfer. Its MSE comes from random synthetic matrices; its trust network is elicited trust among decision-makers, not cosponsorship; its alternatives are 5 investment options, not legislators' CU stance categories. Its homophily premise is assumed, never tested, while this system measured co-movement as null on cosponsor ties. A weighted variant should be adopted only if a masked-cell test beats both the current unweighted mean and a party-only baseline on held-out members. Until a second path reproduces that result it stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062). Weights must be labelled heuristic tie strength, never trust or closeness (D-025).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation|Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation]]

gaps_exposed: The stance-dynamics masking check has no party-only baseline. Neither does the paper's MSE test. Neither can show that network-neighbour imputation adds anything beyond party (this is also the open question listed for the component).

The neighbour imputation ignores tie strength and similarity: binary adjacency gives weak and strong cosponsor ties equal votes. If imputation is kept at all, a weighted or reliability-ordered variant is the untested alternative.
Minor code-label mismatch: the summary print at fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:152 says '>=3 informative neighbors', but the gate MINNB defaults to 5 (line 132).
flags: The paper's 'trust' is an elicited trust degree between decision-makers. Porting its weighting onto cosponsor or staffer edges and calling it trust would break D-025: graph weights are heuristic model outputs, never closeness, access or introduction probabilities.

The paper's KNN imputation assumes preferences are similar among network neighbours, but the system measured cosponsor-tie co-movement as null. Treat any claim that this paper supports neighbour imputation as unsupported for this corpus.

This paper argues for neither rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). It does not use LDA. It reports a reciprocity-like 'mutual influence' term only inside clustering, which gives no support to reciprocity (D-104..D-108 status unchanged).
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation of this paper. For the closest component (stance-dynamics), his note asks for temporal dynamics and change-likelihood modelling, and it predates the null co-movement result. This paper does not resolve that tension. Its neighbour-imputation evidence is synthetic and rests on an assumed homophily the system did not find. His note is stale on that point; nothing in this paper revives the premise.

related.why: The system's stance-dynamics imputer cites Zhou-Elejalde silent-actor collaborative filtering as its template (fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:147). Zhan-Cai gives a trust- and similarity-weighted alternative to the same neighbour-imputation idea.
Cao 2025 is a survey of social-network group decision making, the field this paper belongs to. It places the paper's trust-driven consensus and minimum-cost feedback among related designs.

extraction.venue: Information Fusion, vol. 120, article 103107 (available online 21 March 2025; received 17 Dec 2024, accepted 9 Mar 2025)
extraction.document_type: Review article: narrative literature review with a descriptive bibliometric analysis and a forward-looking research agenda (AI and LLM perspective). No new empirical study.
extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text, all 1,803 lines covering pp.1-18: abstract, introduction, Sections 2-6, CRediT, declarations, and all references. Figures 1-8 appear in the text file only as captions, so the numbers inside Figs 2-5 (publication and citation counts, journal counts, author clusters, keyword network) are not available here. Paul's markup: the file list is "(none)". I also searched the _annots folder for the hash f087daf89a1e; no annotation file references this paper, so paul_markup is empty. Metadata hint checked: author list and year match the paper; the DOI was blank in the hint and is filled from the text (p.1).
extraction.research_question: What is social network group decision making (SNGDM), and how should it be defined, characterized and classified? The paper aims to (1) give a formal definition and characterization of the SNGDM framework relative to classical group decision making; (2) map the literature as a taxonomy of trust modeling, internal network structure and consensus mechanisms; and (3) set out challenges and future directions, including how AI, large language models (LLMs) and multimodal fusion could be used. Stated in the Introduction, pp.2-3.
extraction.data: Literature records, not primary data. Bibliometric unit: journal article records from the Web of Science. Raw retrieval: 11,090 records (search window stated as 1990-2024; search snapshot 25 Sept 2024). After manual title/abstract screening: 1,800. After removing duplicates across the four searches: 917 unique articles, which form the bibliometric base (pp.3-4). Table 1 (raw / after screening) by keyword pair: 'Social network' & 'Consensus' 2,720 / 466; 'Social network' & 'GDM' 2,722 / 687; 'Trust' & 'Consensus' 2,776 / 306; 'Trust' & 'GDM' 2,872 / 341; total 11,090 / 1,800; de-duplicated 917. The paper states "No data was used for the research described in the article" (p.16).
extraction.method: Narrative review organized as a taxonomy: trust modeling (representation, propagation, evolution), internal structure (consensus measurement, power structure, community structure), and consensus mechanisms (feedback, opinion dynamics, behavior management). Bibliometric step (Section 2.2, p.3): Web of Science Boolean searches on four keyword pairs, manual screening using field and institution shortcuts plus abstract reading, de-duplication. Descriptive outputs only: publications and average citations per year (Fig 2), journals (Fig 3), co-author clusters (Fig 4), keyword co-occurrence (Fig 5). Sections 4 and 5 are agenda-setting arguments with no models fitted or tested. Section 5 covers LLMs and multimodal fusion conceptually; no experiment is run.
extraction.identification: None. The paper makes no causal or statistical identification claim. It is a descriptive review and bibliometric mapping.
extraction.scope: Population: decision-making research on social network group decision making indexed in Web of Science, search window 1990-2024, snapshot 25 Sept 2024. The abstract calls the window "the past decade"; Section 2.2 uses 1990-2024. Institution: none (WoS only). Era: pre-LLM literature plus a 2024-2025 forward look at LLMs, multimodal models and small language models. Applications used as examples: village chief elections (p.3, illustrative), urban renewal, water-pollution compensation, vaccine uptake (p.1), disaster response, online product reviews, household energy use, and physicians' adoption of online health communities (p.13). No lobbying, campaign, legislator, turnout or persuasion literature is reviewed beyond these examples.

key_findings.finding: Definition 1: an SNGDM event needs at least three decision-makers evaluating alternatives, plus a network among them (nodes, edges, edge weights) that shapes information exchange and the outcome. The authors say SNGDM is more than GDM plus social networks because the two processes are coupled.
key_findings.location: p.3, Definition 1 and Section 2.1.1 (lines 214-220); coupling claim p.2 (lines 84-86)

key_findings.finding: Bibliometric base: four Web of Science keyword pairs returned 11,090 records, manual screening kept 1,800, and de-duplication left 917 articles. The search counts are in Table 1.

Origin: Wu and Chiclana (2014, Knowl.-Based Syst. 59) first presented SNGDM. Papers from the inaugural year have the highest average citations, which the authors read as showing the earliest work is of high academic value. Figure values are not in the text.

Keyword analysis: current SNGDM research centers on decision-making methods, social network analysis and consensus-reaching processes. The authors call trust behavior a deeper issue that is gaining importance.

Trust representation is classified into four types: binary (trust/distrust), multi-discrete levels, continuous values, and fuzzy-logic values (interval values, intuitionistic fuzzy numbers, trust score spaces).

Trust propagation is characterized by four properties (symmetry, follow-through, directness, divergence). Two approaches are named: propagation operators (six families listed) and trust aggregation over multiple paths.

Trust decay along propagation chains is an active line of work: discount-factor and exponential-decay operators penalize long chains. The authors call for systematic study of decay drivers such as path length and node importance, and of how these affect trust network reliability.
key_findings.location: p.7 (lines 498-510); long-chain propagation effect in Tan et al. at p.7 (lines 493-495)

key_findings.finding: Consensus measurement: the authors judge a combined measure of opinion similarity and trust, covering within-subgroup consensus, between-subgroup consensus and trust among members, to be the reasonable approach.

Overlapping communities: Gai et al. (ref [60]) report that overlapping communities raise experts' willingness to compromise relative to non-overlapping communities. The authors treat overlapping nodes as bridges, an area they say needs more work.
Pseudoconsensus: clustering strengthens homogeneity within subgroups but also heterogeneity between them, so high within-subgroup consensus may not mean good overall consistency.

Behavior management: weight manipulation and non-cooperative behavior are treated as threats to consensus. Yang et al. (ref 26) define three non-cooperative categories: bribery, passive participation and potential conflict. The authors argue these should be addressed by regulating trust relations.
key_findings.location: p.10-11, Section 3.3.3 (lines 860-955); Yang et al. at p.11 (lines 938-941)

key_findings.finding: Future directions in SNGDM methods: trust incentives with personality types, trust games, implicit power of trust, crowd wisdom, reinforcement-learning feedback, personality-trait learning via multimodal sentiment analysis, online-review-driven SNGDM, and realistic scenario-driven SNGDM. Each is proposed, not tested.

LLM and multimodal opportunities are listed in six application areas: public opinion monitoring, recommendation, emergency decision making, policy evaluation, communication support, and ethics and fairness.

Technological challenges for LLM and multimodal SNGDM are listed as five areas: data heterogeneity, adaptability and generalization, computational cost, lack of unified evaluation standards, and use of small language models.

Conclusion: LLMs, multimodal fusion and AI are named among the main future directions for SNGDM. The authors also raise the need for transparent, ethical and adaptable autonomous AI agents for group consensus, subject to regulation.

summary_md:
Cao et al. (2025, Information Fusion) is a narrative review plus a descriptive bibliometric map of "social network group decision making" (SNGDM). It reports no new data and fits no model. It defines an SNGDM event as at least three decision-makers whose trust or social network shapes how they reach consensus on alternatives. It classifies the literature along three axes: trust modelling (representation, propagation, decay), internal structure (consensus measurement, power, communities) and consensus mechanisms (feedback, DeGroot or Hegselmann-Krause opinion dynamics, managing manipulation or non-cooperation). It then lists directions for LLMs and multimodal methods. The bibliometric base is 917 Web of Science articles (11,090 raw records, 1,800 after screening; snapshot 25 Sept 2024). Every substantive claim is either a taxonomy label or an agenda item. Nothing is estimated, and the authors say no unified standard exists for evaluating LLM or multimodal SNGDM.

For Paul's systems, this paper is a vocabulary source, not evidence. Three points come close to built components. First, it names multiplicative discount-factor trust propagation and calls decay along chains (path length, node importance) systematically unstudied. That describes the uncalibrated 0.8-per-hop factor and 5-year half-life in the staffer router, and the ASKM product in the recruitment chain. Second, it separates single-path propagation operators from trust aggregation over multiple paths. The member recruitment chain uses only the single most reliable path and says in its own comment that this is a floor. Third, its "pseudoconsensus" warning says high agreement inside a subgroup need not mean agreement between subgroups. That fits the Ward press-lean blocs, which are all labelled pro-CU. Its SNGDM populations are small expert panels with elicited or preset trust, not legislators, staffers or lobbyists, so nothing in it validates any constant. All bearings are weak and UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Discount-factor and exponential-decay operators penalize long trust chains, but the drivers of decay (path length, node importance) and their effect on network reliability have not been systematically modelled. Narrative claim only; no decay rate is estimated.
bearings.system_side: Access uncertainty is an exploratory log-cost: cost = 0.35 + ln2 x years since overlap / 5 + 0.25 x workplace concentration, and factor = exp(-cost). The code says this is not a probability. Route hops add -ln(0.8 x strength), so each hop discounts by a fixed factor of 0.8.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the taxonomy transfers: the system uses a fixed-discount, exponential-decay operator of the kind the review names, and the review confirms that no literature-standard decay rate exists. SNGDM trust is trust elicited inside small expert panels. Staffer edges are dated employment exposure. Neither the 0.8 hop factor nor the 5-year half-life gains or loses support from this paper. Route costs stay heuristic and are never closeness or introduction probabilities (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: Trust propagation is done either with propagation operators along one path (six operator families) or by aggregating trust over multiple paths. Propagation has four properties: symmetry, follow-through, directness and divergence. Sun et al. (2023) and Tan et al. (2022) study optimal paths and long-chain effects.
bearings.system_side: The chain uses the single most reliable path: Dijkstra on -log p, then chainHold = product of activeP(p) per hop, with ASKM 0.07. The code comment calls this a conservative floor because rerouting only improves it. Multi-path aggregation (cov = 1 - prod(1-p)) appears only in budgetRecruit coverage, not in the reported chain hold.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Taking a product along one path is the multiplicative operator family the review lists. Aggregating over alternative paths would turn the floor into a fuller estimate. This only matters if the edge probabilities mean something empirically, and the cosponsor-kernel p and ASKM are uncalibrated. The paper offers a concept, not evidence that multi-path aggregation predicts real recruitment.

bearings.paper_claim: Pseudoconsensus: clustering raises homogeneity within subgroups but also heterogeneity between them, so high internal consensus need not mean the subgroups agree with one another.
bearings.system_side: Ward.D2 clusters member press-lean profiles into 9 blocs, with COALITION_LEAN_WEIGHT 3.0 and a minimum of 6 members, as a static snapshot. The brain records that every bloc is labelled pro-CU, which is a known mislabel.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The point is logical, not empirical, so it carries over to any clustering. Agreement within a bloc says nothing about alignment across blocs or with CU positions. A bloc label needs a between-bloc check of direction against an external criterion such as votes. No numbers transfer.

bearings.paper_claim: SNGDM consensus mechanisms model opinion updating along trust edges with DeGroot and Hegselmann-Krause dynamics (refs 9 and 71). The review treats network-driven opinion convergence as the core mechanism but reports no test of it.
bearings.system_side: Neighbour imputation takes an unweighted mean of neighbours' tier scores, which is one DeGroot-style averaging step. It requires at least 5 neighbours (MINNB) and |est| >= 0.75 (CONF), and it only proposes values without changing the matrix. Measured co-movement on the cosponsor and HCoI layers was null.
bearings.transfer_conditions: DeGroot assumes that neighbours' opinions move a node's opinion. That holds by design in elicited SNGDM panels. The system's own null co-movement result means the assumption is not supported on congressional layers. This paper adds no evidence either way, so the imputation stays a proposal-only heuristic.

gaps_exposed: No multi-path aggregation in the reported member recruitment chain hold. The system reports only the single best path's product, which the code itself calls a floor.

No calibrated per-hop decay anywhere: the staffer HOP_FACTOR 0.8, the 5-year access half-life and ASKM 0.07 are all unestimated. The review confirms the field has no standard to borrow, so calibration would need the system's own outcome data, such as an outreach log.
No check of direction between blocs for press-lean Ward blocs (the pseudoconsensus risk), consistent with the recorded all-pro-CU mislabel.
flags: The review contains no evidence about legislators, staffers or lobbying. Any citation of it as support for route costs, trust decay or recruitment probabilities would break D-025: route costs and graph scores are heuristics, not closeness or introduction probabilities.
Neither rejected SNA proposal is argued for (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). Nothing to flag on that front.

Section 3.3.3 frames 'bribery' and weight manipulation as threats to consensus. This is SNGDM vocabulary about expert panels. It must not carry over as influence or vote-buying language onto money or revolving-door edges.

Incidental code observation, not from the paper: fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:152 prints 'cells with >=3 informative neighbors', but the gate at line 132 defaults MINNB to 5. The log string is stale against the code.
All bearings here are new single-path agent analysis and stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper, and no position card cites it. Two of his stated wants are close to it. One is relationship decay, under staffer access-uncertainty, where his note says no source estimates a staffer-tie half-life. The review agrees: it says trust-propagation decay is not yet systematically modelled, so his note stands and is not stale. The other is path-finding robust to unstable information. The review's distinction between multi-path and single-path propagation fits that want, but it supplies no method he could adopt directly. Nothing here contradicts his positions. The paper's LLM agenda does echo his interest in LLM readers, but it gives no validation numbers, unlike Birkenmaier or Kim.

related.why: A primary SNGDM paper (large-scale group decision making with trust networks and consensus feedback) in the literature this review classifies. It is the concrete method instance behind the review's consensus-mechanism taxonomy.
Most-reliable-path is the single-path multiplicative operator the review lists. Together they frame the choice between single-path and multi-path propagation for the recruitment chain.
Strongest-path search over social tie strength corresponds to the review's trust-propagation operators and path-length decay concern.
Zhou's temporal-graph stance dynamics is the source for the system's neighbour imputation. The review's DeGroot or Hegselmann-Krause framing is the opinion-dynamics theory behind that imputation.
Signed partitioning between subgroups addresses the review's pseudoconsensus concern, that internal homogeneity is not cross-group agreement.

extraction.title: Efficient Influence Maximization in Social-Networks Under Independent Cascade Model
extraction.venue: Procedia Computer Science 173 (2020) 315-324, ICITETM2020 (International Conference on Smart Sustainable Intelligent Computing and Applications). Metadata hint verified against the PDF header and first page.
extraction.document_type: Conference paper (open access, CC BY-NC-ND), 10 pages incl. references
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass (text file lines 1-475: front matter, abstract, Sections 1-5, all 22 references). Coverage of the topics the brief names: influence maximization and seed selection (full), independent cascade and threshold models (full), greedy/CELF/centrality methods (full), networks and path-finding (Chen et al. maximum-influence-path mention, p.318; no original path-finding contribution). Lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators, allocation under budget, and text measurement: NOT present in the paper. The abstract mentions selecting k users at minimum cost, and p.318 says the problem can be generalized to cost, but no cost model is built or tested.
extraction.research_question: Given a social network and a diffusion model, which k seed nodes maximize expected spread under the Independent Cascade Model (ICM) while keeping computation cheap? Two sub-questions: (a) can a degree-based heuristic (DHICM) approach greedy/CELF spread at much lower cost; (b) can ICM edge probabilities be derived from network structure (degrees, common neighbours) instead of a fixed constant, to make spread more realistic (MICM).
extraction.theory: Independent Cascade and Linear Threshold diffusion models (Kempe et al. 2003, ref [12]); word-of-mouth and viral-marketing theory (Goldenberg et al. 2001, refs [6][7] as cited; Granovetter 1978 for thresholds); submodularity of the spread function, which gives the greedy (1-1/e, text says 63%) guarantee (p.318); degree-discount heuristic (Chen et al. 2009, ref [4]); the claim that centrality heuristics are fast and that similarity (degree and common neighbours) can proxy real propagation probability (p.320-321).
extraction.data: Two academic co-authorship networks, labelled NetHept and NetPhy, with the authors citing ref [20] (Wang, Chen, Wang 2012) for the source. Unit: author = node; edge = two authors who co-wrote a paper. Both are undirected multigraphs that the authors simplify to undirected simple graphs (p.322). Table 4.1 (p.322): NetHept n = 15,233 nodes, m = 58,891 edges; NetPhy n = 37,154 nodes, m = 231,584 edges. Abstract says the academic collaboration data is from arXiv.org; the text does not name the arXiv subject categories. Time period: not stated. Hardware: 2.10 GHz Xeon, 6 cores / 12 logical processors, 16 GB RAM (p.321). No real diffusion or outcome data is used; all results are simulated spread on the networks.
extraction.method: Algorithmic benchmark with Monte Carlo simulation of ICM. (1) DHICM (Algorithm 3, p.320): compute degrees, then repeatedly pick the max-discounted-degree node and update each un-seeded neighbour v as dd_v = d_v - 1 - (d_u - 1)p (Eq. 3.2), where p is the ICM propagation probability. Stated complexity O(n + k log n + m). (2) MICM (Eq. 3.3, p.320): edge probability p_ij = 0.01 + (d_i + d_j)/n + CN(i,j)/n, with n the node count and CN the common-neighbour count (the extracted equation is typeset ambiguously; this is the reading the surrounding prose gives). Spread is estimated by R Monte Carlo runs per candidate (Algorithm 2, p.319); the value of R used in experiments is NOT reported. Baselines: CELF (Leskovec et al. 2007, ref [13]), degree centrality, Katz centrality, PrKatz (ref [1] as cited), and Random. k is varied (values shown in figures for k = 10 to 80). Baseline ICM uses p = 0.01 (Fig. 4.1 caption, p.322).
extraction.identification: None. The paper makes no causal claim; it is a comparative simulation benchmark. The "modified ICM" is an assumed functional form for edge probability, justified by prose (similarity, real-world dynamics), not estimated from data or validated against observed diffusion.
extraction.scope: Population: two academic co-authorship networks (no social media or political networks). Institution: National Institute of Technology Delhi (authors); conference ICITETM2020. Era: not stated. Generalization is limited to ICM with the two networks tested; the authors themselves say performance on other cascade models is untested (p.324).

key_findings.finding: DHICM spread on NetHept is close to CELF: 12.5% lower at k=10 and 7.9% lower at k=30.
DHICM beats degree centrality on NetHept for every k tested.
On NetPhy, DHICM beats degree centrality at k=50 and trails CELF slightly at k=30.
key_findings.numbers: k=50: +10% vs degree; k=30: -2.5% vs CELF

key_findings.finding: PrKatz (Katz-based, ref [1]) underperforms: on NetHept it is worse than Random for some k; on NetPhy it beats Random throughout. Authors attribute this to graph pre-processing that splits the graph into components and to Katz centrality being weaker than degree in their results.
key_findings.numbers: not reported as a table value; qualitative

key_findings.finding: Running time: CELF takes very large time on both datasets; DHICM takes a few seconds more than plain degree and Katz centrality.
key_findings.numbers: times shown only in figures; no numeric table

key_findings.finding: Modified ICM (MICM) raises spread for every algorithm on NetHept. Katz +5.7% at k=30; Degree +8.92% at k=70; DHICM +6.8% at k=40; CELF +12.5% at k=70.
On NetPhy under MICM, gains are much larger: Katz +31.29% (k=20); Degree +32.60% (k=20); DHICM +23.7% (k=30); CELF +55.55% (k=10).

MICM raises run time: DHICM +12.6% (NetHept) and +8.6% (NetPhy); CELF +9.4% and +6.5%; degree and Katz no significant change. Authors attribute the increase to larger spread, not to a complexity change.
Stated complexity: DHICM O(n + k log n + m) vs greedy O(knRm) (R = Monte Carlo runs). Conclusion restates CELF as O(nkRm); the two complexity statements are not identical.
Authors' main conclusion: centrality heuristics should be improved rather than making greedy faster, and edge probabilities should be derived from node or network information.

measures: Expected spread Gamma(S): number of active nodes at end of ICM cascade from seed set S, estimated by Monte Carlo (p.317-318)
Marginal influence Minf(u) = |Gamma(S u {u}) - Gamma(S)| (Eq 2.1, p.318)
Degree centrality d_v; degree-discount dd_v (Eq 3.1-3.2, p.319-320)
Katz centrality (ref [22]) and PrKatz pre-processed Katz (ref [1])
Edge propagation probability p_ij from degrees and common neighbours (Eq 3.3)
Wall-clock running time in seconds (Fig 4.2, 4.4)
Percentage gain of MICM over ICM for each algorithm (Sec 4.2)
limitations: Only ICM tested; authors state DHICM performance must be tested on other cascade models (p.324).
Only two co-authorship networks; no node attributes used by design (p.320: only topology assumed known). Generalization to other network types is untested.
MC sample size R used in experiments is not reported; no error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated-seed runs in the text, so the reported percentage differences cannot be checked for noise.
Baseline ICM uses p = 0.01 for all edges, which the authors themselves call unrealistically low (p.321); MICM gains are measured against this weak baseline.

MICM edge probability (Eq 3.3) is an ad hoc functional form with no empirical validation against real diffusion data; the claim that it reflects real-world dynamics (p.321, p.323) is asserted, not tested. The 0.01 constant and normalisation by n are chosen by the authors.
Gains from MICM are reported as percent increases in spread without showing that the ranking of algorithms is unchanged; some MICM rankings (e.g. CELF vs DHICM) are not discussed.
Network simplification: multigraphs turned into simple graphs (p.322), so repeated co-authorship weights are discarded.
Complexity claims are inconsistent: O(knRm) (p.320) vs O(nkRm) for CELF (p.323); and the stated DHICM complexity is not validated by any timing scaling experiment.
PrKatz is re-implemented by the authors, and they state their results show it underperforms; no details are given on the re-implementation.

Citation numbering in the text does not match the reference list: text cites [2] for Goldenberg et al. (list [2] is Arora et al.) and [17] for Kempe et al. (list [17] is Richardson and Domingos). Read the reference list with care.
Abstract says DHICM spread is 'close to benchmark greedy', but this is shown only on two networks and only with the greedy approximated by CELF.
references_of_note: Kempe, Kleinberg, Tardos 2003, 'Maximizing the spread of influence through a social network' (ref [12]): defines ICM and LTM, proves NP-hardness and submodularity, greedy (1-1/e, text says 63%) guarantee.

summary_md:
Trivedi and Singh (2020) is a short algorithm benchmark under the Independent Cascade Model (ICM). It makes two proposals. The first, DHICM, extends Chen et al.'s 2009 degree-discount rule: once a node is picked as a seed, each neighbour's degree is discounted by dd_v = d_v - 1 - (d_u - 1)p. The second, MICM, replaces the constant edge probability (p = 0.01) with a structural form: 0.01 + (d_i + d_j)/n + common neighbours/n. Both are tested on two arXiv co-authorship graphs (NetHept: 15,233 nodes and 58,891 edges; NetPhy: 37,154 nodes and 231,584 edges). The data contain no real diffusion or outcomes, and the paper does not report how many Monte Carlo runs it used or give error bars. On NetHept, DHICM's spread is 12.5% below CELF at k=10 and 7.9% below at k=30. It beats plain degree centrality by 10 to 16% and runs in seconds where CELF takes far longer. A Katz-based heuristic does worse than degree and sometimes worse than random. MICM raises spread for every algorithm (CELF by up to +55.6% on NetPhy at k=10). That rise mostly follows mechanically from leaving a deliberately low 0.01 baseline, and the paper offers no evidence that MICM is realistic.

For Paul's system the paper matters mainly as a calibration of trade-offs. With 533 members and a stance-gated shortlist of 45, CELF's cost does not constrain the budget frontier, so the paper's 8 to 12% spread penalty argues for keeping the exact lazy greedy over a degree heuristic. The dashboard's budget-recruit mode is already a probabilistic one-hop degree-discount, which is the DHICM family. The per-topic coalition allocator scores each candidate's marginal in isolation and ignores seed overlap, which is the problem degree-discount exists to fix. MICM does not calibrate the kernel: the system draws edge probabilities from weighted cosponsorship with saturation, at much higher p than 0.01. All spread figures here are simulated model outputs on co-authorship graphs, not measured influence.

extraction.title: How Dark Is It? An Investigation of Dark Money Operations in U.S. Nonprofit Political Advocacy Organizations
extraction.venue: Nonprofit Policy Forum 14(2): 101-129 (received July 15, 2022; accepted February 28, 2023)
extraction.document_type: Peer-reviewed journal article; empirical index construction and validation (open access, CC BY 4.0)
extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text in two chunks (lines 1-1591 and 1592-2172 of 2172), covering abstract, introduction, theory, context, sample, index construction (all nine components), correlation tables, results, OpenSecrets validation, discussion, conclusion and references. Paul's markup: no markup files were listed for this PDF (task specified "(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. Extracted tables 2-4 are garbled in the text layer (cell values largely missing), so table-level numbers are not reconstructed beyond what the prose states.
extraction.research_question: Can observable characteristics in IRS Form 990 filings and one website measure be combined into a transparency (versus opaqueness) index that ranks social welfare 501(c)(4) economic policy advocacy organizations on how likely they are to be vehicles for dark money political activity? Secondary: under what conditions would a high net worth donor benefit from keeping advocacy operations low-profile (p.105-106)?
extraction.theory: Combined theory. (1) Elite theory (Gen and Wright 2018): political power is held by a small upper-class segment with uniform preferences that intentionally perpetuates its privileges. (2) Weisbrod (1991) heterogeneous-preferences model: a median voter sets the level of tax-funded service provision; donors with preferences far from the median can fund advocacy to move the median voter. Combined, elites may move the median voter away from the median position and have reasons to stay invisible: insider tactics can yield only temporary wins if voters later punish lawmakers (p.104-105); unpopular causes need broad support, so a funder's identity is a liability (astroturf and authenticity, Walker 2014; "big bad opponent," Gen and Wright 2018; local-donor trust in high-stakes races; avoiding association with negative messaging) (p.105-106).
extraction.data: Unit: organization (social welfare 501(c)(4) advocacy organizations active in U.S. or state-level economic policy). N = 54 organizations: 25 right-leaning, 2 centrist, 27 left-leaning (p.110). Sources: IRS Form 990 (Part I lines 4, 6, 9, 15, 16b, 18; Part IX line 11d; Part X line 27; Schedule C Part I-A line 1; Schedule R), website word counts (Weglot counter; seven sites hand-counted), Form 990 expense data for 2015 and 2016, and the OpenSecrets 2016 dark-money list (95 organizations nationally; 13 of the 54 sample organizations appear). Period: fiscal data for 2016 (presidential election year), with 2015 comparison for expense growth; economic policy verbiage checked for 2017; the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (December 2017) context. Sample rules: founded 2015 or earlier; 2016 total revenue above $100,000; at least four economic policy items on website (testimony, podcasts, blogs, research reports, convenings, press releases) in 2017; sourced from think-tank lists, partisan networks, Post and Boris (2020), and donor-advised fund grantee lists. Author states the dataset covers the population of active organizations in this arena in 2016 (p.110-111). U.S. data only.
extraction.method: Descriptive and correlational index construction. Nine components each scaled to 0-1 and summed (maximum 9.0, unweighted by design). Pearson bivariate correlation matrix among components (Table 2, two-tailed significance). Validation against an external watchdog label: second Pearson matrix of the OpenSecrets binary designation against the nine components, plus a logistic regression of OpenSecrets designation on the total index with controls for political lean, natural log of total expenses and founding year; Nagelkerke R-squared reported (p.124). Qualitative case discussion of high-index organizations (p.124-125).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. Validity is assessed by convergent correlation of components with the OpenSecrets dark-money label and a logistic regression with controls. The author notes the sample was chosen by advocacy topic, not by transparency, so the logistic result (index not significant) is interpreted as a sample-design limitation, and validity is argued from component correlations instead (p.124).
extraction.scope: Population: 501(c)(4) social welfare organizations active in U.S. (and state-level) economic policy advocacy, 2016 filings. Institution: U.S. tax-exempt advocacy sector and its links to 501(c)(3) think tanks, 527 organizations and Super PACs. Era: 2015-2017 data, published 2023. The author argues the index transfers to other issue areas (education, Social Security, energy, judicial reform, voting restrictions) but this is not tested (p.109, 125).

key_findings.finding: Index values range from 0.8 (Fix the Debt Coalition Inc.) to 8.3 (Majority Forward), out of a possible 9.0.

Index bands: up to 3.0 transparent; 3.0-5.0 some opaque characteristics (contentious band; includes Americans for Prosperity and Open Society Policy Center); 5.0-7.0 quite opaque; above 7.0 very opaque, including many large advocacy groups with very small boards, sparse websites and no staff.
Anomaly cases: One Nation spent $63.3M in 2016 (up from $7.1M in 2015), had one board member, and gave $21.7M to the Senate Leadership Fund (PAC at the same address).
Majority Forward spent $35.8M in 2016 with salaries at 1.34% of expenses, an 81-word website and two board members.

Freedom Frontier spent $5.9M in 2016 (up from $873,707 in 2015); $6.2M of revenue came entirely from grants and contributions with no fundraising expense; almost 75% of expenses went to political activity, including a $4.4M grant to a PAC.
Organizations rely heavily on donated revenue, averaging 92% of total revenue; the data cannot show whether that comes from few large donors or many small donors.
key_findings.numbers: mean 92% of revenue from grants and contributions

key_findings.finding: Almost all index components are positively correlated with each other; the single negative correlation is not significant. Salaries as a percent of expenses is the component most strongly correlated with the others.
Only two organizations had membership revenue (Maine People's Alliance; Utah Taxpayers Association), so membership was dropped from the index.
Three mid-sized organizations had boards of 26, 34 and 37 members, truncated to 25 for the board component.
Two organizations had fundraising expenses exceeding grants and contributions; that component was truncated at zero.

Validation: 13 of the 54 sample organizations appear on the OpenSecrets 2016 dark-money list of 95 national groups. The OpenSecrets binary label is significantly correlated with four components: related to a 527, political spending as a percent of expenses, salaries as a percent of expenses, and unrestricted net assets as a percent of expenses.

key_findings.finding: Logistic regression of OpenSecrets designation on the total index (controls: lean, ln total expenses, founding year) is not significant for the index. key_findings.finding: Political spending across this sample is described as strongly negative, asking voters to defeat candidates, per FEC filings reported by Beckel (2018).
key_findings.numbers: qualitative; no count given in text

key_findings.finding: Expenses rose sharply between 2015 and 2016 (a presidential year). The author considered an expense-growth component and excluded it because political spending peaks in presidential years for any organization.

Context: in the year before the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (December 2017), polls showed broad majority support for raising taxes on the wealthy (Gallup 2017; Pew 2017; Reuters/Ipsos 2017), and the author treats the 2016 set as a window onto a conservative tax-policy win.

Author concludes high-index C4s look like elite issue entrepreneurs (Goss 2016) under a strict sense: a single donor or few donors may control the C4 as a for-profit firm. Author argues this challenges the C4 definition of promoting general welfare and that C4 use as a conduit around FEC individual limits resembles straw donation; recommends publicly reporting the largest donors behind C4 political funding.

measures: Index (0-9, sum of nine components, unweighted): transparency/opacity composite. Higher = more opaque.
C1 Board size (Form 990 Part I line 4): 1 - min(board size, 25)/25; takes greater of C4 and related 501(c)(3) board.
C2 Volunteers (Part I line 6): 0 if reported 0 or blank, 1 if volunteers used; recorded as one minus value so the scale matches transparency direction.
C3 Website words: 1 - min(word count, 100,000)/100,000; related 501(c)(3) or 527 site used as proxy when C4 has none.
C4 Related to a 527 (Schedule R): 0 if none, 1 if one or more related 527s; scaled to 0-1 in the index.
C5 Related to a 501(c)(3) (Schedule R): 0 if related to one or more 501(c)(3)s, 1 if not.
C6 Grants to political organizations or lobbying scaled by total expenses (Schedule C Part I-A line 1 plus Part IX line 11d); text does not print the exact 0-1 transform for this component.
C7 Salaries: 1 - total salaries (Part I line 15) / total expenses (Part I line 18). Consultant fees excluded unless employee-based; contractor data not split.
C8 Unrestricted net assets (Part X line 27): 1 - UNA / (3 x total expenses), negative UNA set to zero; three years of expenses treated as generous savings target.
C9 Fundraising: 1 - fundraising expenses (Part I line 16b) / grants and contributions (Part I line 9), truncated at zero.
Political-intensity measure (expense increase in presidential vs non-presidential year) and membership revenue were considered and excluded.
Validation label: OpenSecrets 2016 dark-money list (binary).
limitations: No perfect external validation source exists because the process is anonymous; the OpenSecrets list is acknowledged as flawed.
Every component measures legal behavior; concern arises only from combinations, and the author accepts this rests on judgment.

Index construction involves truncation of outliers (board size at 25, website words at 100,000, UNA at 3x expenses, fundraising at zero) that are value judgments; OECD (2008) is cited on weighting and truncation.
Equal weighting is a deliberate simplicity choice, but the author notes organizations would argue for different weights that favor them.
Form 990 data become public only after two or more years, so organizations can operate unscrutinized for a period.
Small N (54) limits statistical power; the logistic regression Nagelkerke R2 of 0.529 is described as reflecting the small dataset; index was not significant against OpenSecrets labels.
Sample was selected on advocacy topic, not on transparency, so the index's validation depends on correlations rather than the OpenSecrets test.
Grants between C4s are not classified as political or issue spending, so some political flows are excluded from C6.
Website word counts are hand-counted for seven sites and use related-organization proxies for some C4s.
Expense and program data are from one presidential year (2016), so cycle-level variation is not modeled.
Fiscal-year and 2017 website verbiage are used for inclusion, so cross-year timing differences are not fully aligned.
Index is applicable only to the U.S. context; generalization to other issue areas is argued but not tested.

summary_md:
Irvin builds a nine-part opacity index from IRS Form 990 fields, plus one website word count, and applies it to 54 501(c)(4) economic-policy advocacy groups using 2016 filings (25 right-leaning, 2 centrist, 27 left-leaning). The components are board size, volunteers, website length, related 527s, related 501(c)(3)s, the share of spending that is political or lobbying, the salary share, the size of reserves and fundraising intensity. Each is scaled 0-1 and the nine are summed with equal weight, so the index runs 0-9. Scores ranged from 0.8 to 8.3. The most opaque groups had one or two board members, almost no staff, very short websites and large grants to affiliated PACs. For example, One Nation spent $63.3M in 2016 and granted $21.7M to the Senate Leadership Fund. Validation is weak. Thirteen of the 54 groups appear on OpenSecrets' 2016 dark-money list, and that label correlates with four of the nine components. But in a logistic regression with controls, the total index does not predict the label (Nagelkerke R2 0.529; only log expenses is significant). The paper also describes this political spending as mostly negative, based on Beckel 2018, without a count.

For Paul's systems this matters mainly in Mentat. The transfer graph traces only FEC committee-to-committee transfers (24G/24K). Money a 501(c)(4) gives a Super PAC therefore enters as a receipt with no upstream path. Separately, under Paul's 2026-07-18 ruling, 501c recipients are excluded from reported totals. The paper shows that excluded group mixes transparent policy shops with near-shell political vehicles. It does not show that the index can tell them apart reliably. Nothing in the paper bears on Melange's member ranking, stance, SNA or Terrier.

extraction.title: Adaptive Submodularity: Theory and Applications in Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization
extraction.venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, vol. 42, pp. 427-486 (2011); extended version of a Conference on Learning Theory 2010 paper (pp. 333-345). Text copy is arXiv:1003.3967v5 [cs.LG], revised 6 Dec 2017.
extraction.document_type: Journal article (theoretical computer science / AI; approximation-guarantee paper with applications and a small experimental section)
extraction.coverage: Read the entire extracted text file (4,038 lines, 200,087 chars) in chunks: front matter, abstract, Sections 1-14 (pp. 1-36), references (pp. 37-41), and Appendix 15 (pp. 41-60, all proofs including costs, Theorems 38-40, Lemmas 36-51, and the Theorem 26 hardness proof). Figures 1-6 are read only through their extracted captions and axis text; numeric values plotted in Figure 5 are not in the text layer. Metadata hint corrected: the venue is JAIR 42 (2011), not just the arXiv number; the copyright line reads 2012. Paul's markup: no annotation file keyed to this document exists in research\_annots or research\annotations, so paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: Can the diminishing-returns property of classical submodular set functions be generalized to adaptive policies, so that a simple adaptive greedy policy is near-optimal for partially observable stochastic maximization, minimum-cost coverage and min-sum cover problems, with applications to sensor placement, stochastic set cover, viral marketing and active learning?
extraction.theory: Adaptive submodularity (Definition 3, Eq. 11, p. 8): for partial realizations psi subset psi', the conditional expected marginal benefit Delta(e|psi) of any fixed item e must satisfy Delta(e|psi) >= Delta(e|psi'). It is defined relative to a known prior distribution p(phi) over realizations, and reduces to classical submodularity when the prior is deterministic (p. 6-7). Adaptive monotonicity (Definition 2, p. 8) is nonnegativity of Delta(e|psi). Strong adaptive monotonicity and strong adaptive submodularity (Definitions 10 and 12, pp. 13-14) are stronger conditions needed for the average-cost bounds. Pointwise submodularity plus adaptive submodularity implies strong adaptive submodularity (Lemma 39, p. 45). The authors show pointwise submodularity alone does not imply adaptive submodularity (counterexample, p. 14).
extraction.data: Theoretical core: no empirical sample. Items are ground-set elements (e.g., sensor locations, graph nodes, unlabeled examples or hypotheses) with a Bayesian prior over realizations. Experiments (Section 10, pp. 29-32): (a) Intel Research Berkeley temperature data, 46 sensors, sampled every 30 seconds for 5 consecutive days starting 28 Feb 2004, covariance estimated empirically; (b) traffic speed data from 357 sensors on I-880 South, California, working days 6 AM-11 AM for one month. Unit of analysis: sensor location (item) and realization. The Figure 5 experiments use a 50% (p_fail = 0.5) failure rate; the lazy-evaluation curves are averaged over 100 runs (temperature) and 10 runs (traffic) per Figure 5 captions.
extraction.method: Formal analysis: define policies over partial realizations, define adaptive monotonicity and submodularity, prove greedy guarantees by a Nemhauser-style argument extended to adaptive policies (Theorem 5 with a lemma on budgeted policies), average- and worst-case cover bounds via a charging/integration argument (Theorems 13-14, Lemma 47), a min-sum bound via a geometric argument of Feige et al. (2004) (Theorem 15), data-dependent upper bounds via a greedy linear program (Lemma 6, Lemma 37, Algorithm 3), a lazy/accelerated greedy (Algorithm 2), application reductions (Sections 6-9), a gap construction (Theorem 25), and a hardness reduction from a permanent-based puzzle (Feige and Lund 1997) with treasure-hunting instances (Theorem 26). Empirical part: Gaussian-process entropy objective I(X_V; Y_A) for sensor selection with failure probability, comparing naive vs. lazy adaptive greedy by wall-clock time and count of objective evaluations, and comparing the data-dependent bounds beta_avg to the greedy reward.
extraction.identification: Not applicable. This is a theoretical approximation-guarantee paper; no causal identification strategy. Guarantees are conditional on the adaptive submodularity property holding with respect to the stated (known) prior p(phi), and on complexity-theoretic assumptions for the hardness results.
extraction.scope: Scope is the class of adaptive stochastic optimization problems over finite item sets with known priors (sensor placement with unreliable sensors; stochastic set cover; adaptive influence/viral marketing under the independent cascade model with full-adoption feedback; pool-based active learning and generalized binary search; optimal decision trees). No human population, institution, legislature, election, lobbying, or text corpus is studied. Era: conference version 2010, journal 2011, arXiv revision 2017.

key_findings.finding: Adaptive greedy policy with budget k achieves at least (1 - 1/e) of the value of the best adaptive policy for adaptive monotone submodular objectives; an alpha-approximate greedy policy achieves (1 - e^{-l/(alpha k)}) when run for l steps.
Adaptive submodularity generalizes classical submodularity; for deterministic priors it reduces to the classical notion, and the greedy guarantee of Nemhauser et al. (1978) carries over.

Average-cost minimum cover: greedy policy costs at most alpha * cavg(opt) * (ln(Q/(delta*eta)) + 1)^2 in general instances, and alpha * cavg(opt) * (ln(Q/eta) + 1)^2 for self-certifying instances. Worst-case cost bound (Theorem 14) is alpha * cwc(opt) * (ln(Q/(delta*eta)) + 1), with the self-certifying worst-case log bound left open.
key_findings.location: Theorem 13, Section 5.2.1, p. 14; Theorem 14, Section 5.2.2, p. 14; Discussion Section 5.2.3, p. 15
key_findings.numbers: squared-log factor for average cost; single-log factor for worst cost; delta = min prior probability; eta = coverage gap

key_findings.finding: Historical correction: an earlier version claimed logarithmic (not squared-logarithmic) average-cost factors; the authors say the proof was flawed, as pointed out by Nan and Saligrama (2017). Whether the log bounds hold, and whether strong adaptive submodularity is required, are open.

Feige's (1998) Set Cover hardness implies no polynomial-time (1 - epsilon) ln(Q/eta) approximation for self-certifying Adaptive Stochastic Min Cost Cover, and no (1 - epsilon) ln(Q/(delta*eta)) approximation for general instances, under NP not in DTIME(n^{O(log log n)}); the worst-case self-certifying log bound remains open.
Adaptive min-sum cover: greedy policy is a 4 alpha approximation to the min-sum cost (Adaptive Stochastic Min-Sum Cover), extending Feige, Lovasz and Tetali (2004) and Streeter and Golovin (2008).
key_findings.location: Theorem 15, Section 5.3.2, p. 16; proof Section 15.5, pp. 56-57

key_findings.finding: Stochastic submodular maximization with multiple failure types (generalizing Asadpour et al. 2008 all-or-nothing failures): the greedy policy obtains (1 - 1/e) of the best adaptive policy when sensor states are independent and the utility is monotone submodular.

Stochastic set cover with arbitrary per-item set distributions and independent sampling: the adaptive greedy algorithm is a (ln n + 1)^2 approximation, where n = |U|, improving on Liu et al. (2008) H_n for two-state items.
key_findings.location: Corollary 18, Section 7.1, p. 19; Liu et al. comparison p. 19

key_findings.finding: Adaptive viral marketing under the independent cascade model with full-adoption feedback is adaptive submodular for any monotone submodular reward, so greedy seeding achieves 1 - 1/e of the best adaptive policy; a minimum-cost cover version has a (ln(Q/eta)+1)^2 guarantee.
key_findings.location: Theorem 19, Section 8.2, p. 21 (proof pp. 21-23); Theorem 20, Section 8.3, p. 23

key_findings.finding: The authors retract an earlier claim that viral marketing is adaptive submodular under the myopic feedback model, giving a 3-node counterexample (edges u->v with p=1 and v->w with p=1-epsilon); they conjecture a constant-factor greedy guarantee still holds there.

key_findings.numbers: p_uv = 1, p_vw = 1 - epsilon; Delta(w|psi) = epsilon < 1 = Delta(w|psi')

key_findings.finding: Generalized binary search (GBS) for pool-based active learning with a Bayesian prior: expected number of queries is at most OPT * (ln(1/min_h p_H(h)) + 1)^2; with a uniform prior, OPT * (ln(|H|-1)+1)^2; with the modified prior p'(h) proportional to max(p_H(h), 1/|H|^2) the factor becomes O((ln|H|)^2).

key_findings.finding: Gupta et al. (2010) achieve O(log|H|) for active learning / optimal decision trees with non-uniform costs and general priors using a non-greedy algorithm; the paper states this removes the cost and probability dependence from the bound.

Lazy (accelerated) adaptive greedy gives large speedups without loss of solution quality on sensor selection with unreliable sensors, because submodularity lets stale marginal gains serve as upper bounds.

key_findings.finding: Adaptivity gap: for adaptive submodular objectives, the adaptivity gap of Adaptive Stochastic Min-Sum Cover (and of min-cost cover in that instance) is Omega(n / log n), while for Stochastic Set Coverage without multiplicities it is Omega(|E|) (Goemans and Vondrak 2006); for Max-Coverage Asadpour et al. show a 1 - 1/e gap.

Hardness without adaptive submodularity: unless PH = Sigma_2^P, no polynomial-time algorithm approximates Adaptive Stochastic Maximization, Min Cost Coverage, or Min-Sum Cover within O(|E|^{1-epsilon}), even for pointwise modular objectives.

key_findings.finding: Pointwise submodularity alone is not sufficient for adaptive submodularity; counterexample with f(S, phi) = |{e in S: phi(e)=1}| and a two-point prior gives Delta(e|empty) = 1/2 but Delta(e|{(e',1)}) = 1.

limitations: Guarantees hold only for objectives that satisfy adaptive submodularity with respect to a known prior p(phi); the property is distribution-dependent (p. 8), and the authors note an objective can be adaptive submodular under one prior but not another.
The prior is assumed known (footnote 2, p. 4). Robustness to prior error is shown only for multiplicative error alpha = d/c (Section 4.3, p. 9).
Item selection is assumed not to alter the realization, so general POMDPs with action-dependent state changes are outside the framework (Section 3.4, p. 9; Section 13.7, p. 36).
Treasure-hunting-type instances with strong synergies between items are not covered (Section 3.4, p. 9; Theorem 26, p. 33).
The average-cost bounds carry squared-logarithmic factors; the authors say the logarithmic version is open, and that the earlier log-factor proof was flawed (Historical Note, p. 14).
Open: whether strong adaptive submodularity is required for Theorem 13 (p. 14); whether the worst-case self-certifying log bound holds (p. 15).
Myopic-feedback influence model: adaptive submodularity was retracted and only a constant-factor greedy guarantee is conjectured (p. 23).
Greedy guarantees assume exact or alpha-approximate greedy selection; sampled marginal gains give only additive error bounds (Section 5.1, p. 11).
Hardness results rest on complexity assumptions (PH = Sigma_2^P, NP not in DTIME(n^{O(log log n)})), and the Gupta et al. O(log|H|) result is cited rather than proven here (p. 29).

Experiments are limited to two sensor datasets (46-sensor Berkeley temperature; 357-sensor I-880 traffic), with failure probability 0.5 in the reported runs; no statistical tests and no social-network or real-diffusion data are used. The viral-marketing and active-learning applications are analytic, not empirical.
The paper treats uniform-cost items in the main text; cost-sensitive results are deferred to the appendix (Section 2.4, p. 6; Appendix 15).
measures: Expected utility favg(pi) = E[f(E(pi,Phi),Phi)]
Average cost cavg(pi) = expected number of items selected
Worst-case cost cwc(pi) = max over realizations of items selected
Min-sum cost c_Sigma(pi) = sum over t of (E[f(E,Phi)] - favg(pi[<t]))
Conditional expected marginal benefit Delta(e|psi) and policy benefit Delta(pi|psi)
Coverage quota Q and coverage gap eta; minimum prior probability delta = min p(phi)
Mutual information I(X_V; Y_A) = H(X_V) - H(X_V|Y_A) used as the sensor-selection objective
Wall-clock time and number of objective-function evaluations (naive vs. lazy adaptive greedy)
Data-dependent upper bound beta_avg on the optimal expected reward
Version-space prior mass in active learning (GBS), and number of queries in expectation
Adaptivity gap (ratio of optimal non-adaptive to optimal adaptive expected cost)

short_quotes.quote: a simple adaptive greedy algorithm is guaranteed to be competitive with the optimal policy

summary_md:
Golovin and Krause extend the diminishing-returns idea behind submodular set functions to adaptive policies. In their setting you pick an item, observe its random outcome, then pick the next item. If the objective's conditional expected marginal gain never rises as more is observed (adaptive submodularity, which is defined relative to a known prior), then adaptive greedy gets at least (1-1/e) of the best adaptive policy. The paper also gives squared-log bounds for minimum-cost cover, a 4-approximation for min-sum cover, data-dependent upper bounds (Lemma 6), and a lazy greedy variant (Algorithm 2) that ran about 3.5-7x faster on 46 sensors and 30-38x faster on 357 sensors. Its limits matter as much as its results. The prior must be known. Sampled marginal gains carry only additive error bounds. The myopic-feedback influence model was retracted. Without adaptive submodularity, Theorem 26 rules out any polynomial-time approximation within O(|E|^(1-eps)).

For Melange, the paper mainly sets the scope of the allocation tier's guarantees. The joint optimizer (fec/engine/optimize.py) uses lazy greedy and a G-K data-dependent bound. It correctly states that it is not an adaptive policy: `observations` is empty, and modeled threshold conversions void the certificate. In its fixed-state case, the separable concave structure gives an exact grid optimum, which is stronger than (1-1/e). The budget frontier, the coalition allocator and the dashboard's budgetRecruit are a different matter. Each claims or implies submodular guarantees that this paper does not supply, because of MC=20 sampled marginals, a competitive two-colour kernel, per-candidate fac or target-distance weights, and singleton-marginal water-fill. The seed gate's independent per-seed take-up matches the structure of the paper's Theorem 16. None of these systems observes real outcomes, so the adaptive half of the paper is not built. All of this analysis is UNVERIFIED (DE-062): one reading of the code, with no second path.

gaps_exposed: No adaptive loop. No allocator observes real outcomes, such as cosponsorship or vote movement after a contribution or ask, and conditions later picks on them. optimize.py reserves `observations=[]` but never fills it, so the adaptive half of Golovin and Krause (Theorem 5 relative to the best adaptive policy) is unavailable.

No explicit prior over member responses. The adaptive guarantees require a known p(phi). SGATE, seed_prob, DTHRESH and PERS are owner constants with no calibrated distribution, and the prospective H1/H2 contract that could estimate them is unscored (F5 underpowered).

Sampled marginals carry no error control. The frontier and coalition engines rank on MC=20 estimates, while the paper gives only additive-error guarantees for sampled greedy. No MC-size-to-error-bound link is computed beyond the top-k stability check.

Submodularity of the competitive cascade objective is asserted, not tested. That covers the two-colour first-to-reach race with money bystanders filtered by `n not in s` and an order-dependent tie-break. No numeric diminishing-returns probe like optimize.py's concavity_violations() exists for spread().

The adaptivity gap is never measured. Theorem 25 shows adaptive versus non-adaptive cost can differ by Omega(n/log n) in cover problems. The system never estimates how much sequential re-targeting on observed outcomes would be worth.

Min-cost cover versions are not built. A question like 'cheapest set of asks to reach a quota of Q cosponsors' would fall under Theorems 13-14 (squared-log bounds), but only budget-maximization modes exist.

paul_alignment: Partly aligned, and Paul's note is stale on one word: "adaptive". He calls adaptive greedy plus CELF the operational layer. The built joint optimizer does match the CELF half: lazy greedy, plus the G-K data-dependent bound as a diagnostic. In its fixed-state case it is stronger than greedy, because the separable concave objective makes greedy exactly optimal. It is not adaptive in Golovin and Krause's sense. Nothing real is observed, `observations` is empty, and the code itself says replanning after a modeled threshold conversion is not an adaptive policy and voids the certificate. So the paper underwrites the guarantee language only for the fixed-state optimizer. The frontier, coalition and dashboard recruitment heuristics fall outside it as built: sampled MC=20 marginals, weighted selection scores, a competitive kernel, and a singleton-marginal split. Paul expects GCOMB to replace greedy at scale, but this paper gives no reason to: at 533 members, lazy greedy is cheap and exact where it applies. Paul's per-topic-allocators position places these in the 'static and submodular tier', but submodularity is assumed there, not checked. His Chen 2023 note on non-diminishing pressure points the same way, toward objectives outside this paper's class.
